body: Videos (Theora/MP4/WebM) are always in a compressed format, so using on-the-fly gzip compression for them isn't needed.

> I did some testing with the same HTTPRequest settings, and a NestJS app returning a 161 MB .blend file. The difference was a bit smaller for me, but the download rate was around 5x slower with gzip enabled, printing the rate with gdscript below (average over the full download):
> 
> func _process(delta):
> 	if is_downloading:
> 		download_timer += delta
> 		var byte_count := $HTTPRequest.get_downloaded_bytes() as int
> 		print("MB/s: %f" % [float(byte_count) / 1024 / 1024 / download_timer])
> The CPU usage was pretty low overall during the gzip download, but the `node.exe` process used more CPU than Godot in my case. It seemed like Godot was mostly waiting for the data while the server was busy compressing. Increasing the chunkSize parameter for compression on the NestJS side brought the download rate pretty close to the no gzip case:
> 
> async function bootstrap() {
>   const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
>   app.use(compression({
>     threshold: 0,
>     chunkSize: 1024 * 1024 // Added this setting to speed up compression
>   }));
>   await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
> }
> Is the url you're connecting to your own server/code? Is there any chance the compression on the server side is slowing down your download?
> 
> Also, I didn't see as much of a slowdown for text files that compressed well. It might be worth checking how much smaller gzip makes the video files - if the file format already uses compression, gzip might just be adding overhead without reducing the file size/network traffic by much.
